I have farmed this land in Quzhou for over thirty years. I never went to school, but I know the soil here on the North China Plain and I watch the weather every day. My family relies on this land, so I do not take risks with strange crops. Every year I plant winter wheat after National Day and harvest it in early June, then immediately put in summer maize and harvest before October. That is the rotation my parents did, and it is what the grain buyers and the flour mill expect. I have five mu of good flat land, all of it irrigated from the well.

This year I will do the same. In October I will rotary-till the wheat stubble from last year and sow improved wheat seed — about thirty jin per mu, the same variety my neighbors use. I will put down compound fertilizer as basal dressing and topdress with urea in spring when the wheat turns green. Wheat needs water, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the roots, and three more times in spring at jointing, heading, and filling. I will spray pesticides three times to control aphids and powdery mildew.

After I cut the wheat in June, I will not till the field again. I will plant hybrid maize seed directly into the wheat stubble — no-tillage saves time, fuel, and moisture when the summer heat comes. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and irrigate twice, at the jointing and filling stages. Maize also needs three pesticide sprays for borers and weeds. I expect about one thousand jin of wheat and a bit more than one thousand jin of maize per mu. That feeds my family and gives me grain to sell.

decision.reasoning_summary: I stick to the wheat-maize double-cropping system because it is the safest and most familiar practice on the North China Plain. Winter wheat is sown in autumn with rotary tillage, fertilized with compound and urea, irrigated four times, and protected with three pesticide sprays. Summer maize follows immediately after wheat harvest using no-tillage direct seeding to save labor and moisture, with two irrigations and three pesticide sprays. This rotation provides both food security and marketable surplus on my five-mu farm.
